slides.title: Solid equilibria and adsorption
slides.narration:
Welcome to session four, solid equilibria and adsorption. This independent lesson replaces our live class while I attend the E C S meeting. Last week, you used thermodynamic consistency and liquid stability to decide whether a model and a proposed phase state were reasonable. Today, we extend that reasoning to systems containing a solid.

We will distinguish bulk phase equilibrium from surface uptake. We will also separate an equilibrium composition or pressure from the amount of material in each part of a system. The lesson includes two actual Lab demonstrations, your own calculations, and independent investigations. Keep your predictions and your first answers. Correcting an explanation after checking evidence is an important part of the work.

slides.title: Your independent lesson
slides.narration:
Open the six-page practice worksheet and the four-page Lab guide using the links on this slide. Keep both beside the video. The worksheet is your working record, while the guide tells you which controls to use and what each result means.

The worked solutions are available for checking, but attempt each question before opening the corresponding answer. Keep your original response and add a correction, rather than replacing it without explanation. You will first work through Lab ten on bulk solid equilibria, then Lab eleven on adsorption. The demonstrations show the workflow, and the later pauses give you time to reproduce it independently. Save your calculation sheets, comparison tables and study J S O N files together.

slides.title: The study route
slides.narration:
This route combines watching with active work. The fixed work budget is one hundred and twenty minutes, with a separate ten-minute break. The actual recording duration appears on the video page. Together, these make a lesson of approximately three hours, although your own completion time may differ.

Start a timer so you can report your actual study time later. The table follows worksheet order, not video timestamps. Work through the process review and solubility calculation, then the finite vessel balance and Lab ten. After the break, continue with adsorption and Lab eleven. Finish with a new case that you solve before seeing the answer, then submit the exit ticket and feedback. The activities form this week's lesson.

Then identify the constraint that makes a rigid closed vessel different from the fixed-temperature, fixed-pressure examples in Week three.

slides.title: Process check
slides.narration:
Check your classifications. Dissolution of a crystal and sublimation transfer the same substance between bulk phases. Adsorption describes uptake associated with a surface. A chemical reaction would instead change species identities and require additional reaction constraints.

The relevant energy criterion depends on what is fixed. At fixed temperature and pressure, a closed system minimizes Gibbs energy. At fixed temperature and volume, the corresponding potential is Helmholtz energy. In both cases, conserved inventories and the allowed states remain constraints on the minimization.

For an ideal gas mixture, total pressure is the sum of partial pressures. An inert gas can therefore raise total pressure without changing the amount of the subliming species. Keep that distinction visible when we later interpret the Lab output.

slides.title: Pure-solid standard state
slides.narration:
We begin with a solid and a liquid at equilibrium. The chemical potential of the component must be the same in the two present phases. On the liquid side, we write its chemical potential as the pure-liquid reference plus R T times the natural logarithm of x times gamma.

The reference is the subcooled pure liquid at the same temperature and pressure. That reference may be a hypothetical continuation below the melting temperature, but it defines the activity convention consistently. The pure solid has unit activity on its own standard state. Unit activity does not mean that its chemical potential or amount is zero. The equality determines a liquid activity. Determining how many moles occupy each phase still requires a material balance.

slides.title: Solubility equation
slides.narration:
The solubility equation links liquid activity to fusion properties. Read the right-hand side as negative fusion enthalpy divided by R, multiplied by the quantity one over T minus one over the melting temperature. That entire expression is dimensionless.

Use temperature in kelvin and fusion enthalpy in joules per mole. With R in joules per mole per kelvin, the units cancel correctly. The expression assumes constant fusion enthalpy and neglects the heat-capacity correction between solid and liquid. It also assumes the specified pure solid, without solid solutions or chemical reactions.

Below the melting temperature, the reciprocal-temperature difference is positive. The negative sign therefore gives a negative logarithm. For an ideal liquid, that predicts a saturated mole fraction below one.

slides.title: Solubility attempt
slides.narration:
Pause for about six minutes and complete B one and B two on worksheet page one. The synthetic melting temperature is three hundred and fifty kelvin. The fusion enthalpy is ten thousand joules per mole, and the system temperature is three hundred kelvin.

Assume an ideal liquid, so gamma is one. First calculate the exponent in the solubility equation, then take the exponential to obtain the saturated mole fraction. Write the intermediate value so you can check the sign and units later. For B two, decide whether the resulting number gives moles of remaining solid. Explain what additional inventory or composition information you would need. Make that distinction before continuing to the numerical check on the next slide.
slides.pause_instruction: Pause for about 6 minutes. Complete worksheet p. 1, B1–B2 before viewing the check.

slides.title: Solubility check
slides.narration:
The exponent is approximately negative zero point five seven two seven three. Its exponential gives a saturated liquid mole fraction of about zero point five six four. This is a composition within the liquid phase. It does not tell us the number of moles dissolved, the total amount of liquid, or the remaining solid inventory.

For a nonideal liquid, the same thermodynamic relation constrains x times gamma. Since gamma can depend on composition, finding the composition may require solving an implicit equation within the admitted phase model. We still need material balances to determine phase amounts. A eutectic introduces additional solid-phase conditions and a second solubility branch. That extension is available in the optional appendix, but it is not required for today's investigation.

slides.title: Sublimation equilibrium
slides.narration:
Now consider a pure bulk solid in equilibrium with its vapor. Equality of chemical potential applies while both phases are present. With the ideal-gas and solid-pressure approximations stated here, this gives a vapor partial pressure equal to the sublimation pressure at that temperature.

The phrase while solid remains matters. A small initial solid inventory may completely enter the gas phase before the vapor reaches that pressure. The final state can then have a lower partial pressure because there is no bulk solid left to enforce the two-phase equality.

Also note which pressure appears in the condition. It is the partial pressure of the subliming species. An inert gas contributes to total pressure, but it is not part of that species' sublimation inventory.

slides.title: Finite-vessel inventory
slides.narration:
Start the vessel calculation by finding the gas capacity at sublimation equilibrium. Multiply sublimation pressure by accessible gas volume, then divide by R T. Compare that capacity with the total amount of the subliming species.

Gas moles equal the smaller of the available inventory and that capacity. Solid moles are the remaining inventory. Use gas moles in the ideal-gas equation to obtain the species partial pressure, and add the inert contribution only when calculating total pressure.

With kilopascals and liters, R has the numerical value eight point three one four four six in compatible units. The gas chemical potential minus the pure-solid reference, divided by R T, is the natural logarithm of partial pressure divided by sublimation pressure. Zero applies with present solid. A negative value is allowed after solid exhaustion.

slides.title: Inventory worked example
slides.narration:
Follow the worked case at three hundred kelvin, one liter and a sublimation pressure of ten kilopascals. The capacity is ten times one, divided by R times three hundred. This gives approximately zero point zero zero four zero zero nine moles.

An inventory of zero point zero one zero moles exceeds the capacity. About zero point zero zero five nine nine one moles therefore remain solid, and the vapor partial pressure is ten kilopascals. An inventory of zero point zero zero two moles is below capacity. All of it enters the gas phase, giving about four point nine eight nine kilopascals. Adding zero point zero zero two moles of inert gas adds the same pressure contribution at this fixed temperature and volume.

slides.title: Inventory attempt
slides.narration:
Now pause for about ten minutes and complete C one through C three on worksheet page two. This is a different vessel: two liters at three hundred kelvin, with a sublimation pressure of eight kilopascals.

Compare total inventories of zero point zero one zero and zero point zero zero four moles. Calculate the capacity first, then gas amount, remaining solid and species partial pressure. Add zero point zero zero one mole of inert gas to each case and calculate total pressure.

Finally, calculate the natural logarithm of partial pressure divided by sublimation pressure. Explain the difference between the equality condition for a present solid and a valid state at the exhausted-solid boundary. Show your substitutions and units before opening the check.

slides.title: Inventory check
slides.narration:
The gas capacity is approximately zero point zero zero six four one five moles. Therefore, the larger inventory retains about zero point zero zero three five eight five moles of solid and has a species partial pressure of eight kilopascals. The smaller inventory completely vaporizes and gives about four point nine eight nine kilopascals.

The inert contributes about one point two four seven kilopascals in each case. Add that contribution to obtain the total pressures shown in the table. The logarithmic chemical-potential difference is zero with solid present, and about negative zero point four seven two three for the exhausted-solid case. A negative value is appropriate there. Check that gas plus solid equals the volatile-species inventory in each row.

slides.title: Adsorption and bulk phases
slides.narration:
Adsorption describes material associated with a surface. An adsorption isotherm gives uptake as a function of gas pressure at a specified temperature. In this lesson, q is absolute uptake measured in moles per kilogram of adsorbent.

The pressure is the partial pressure of the adsorbate. To turn uptake into an amount in moles, multiply q by the adsorbent mass expressed in kilograms. For example, a value of one mole per kilogram on ten grams of adsorbent corresponds to zero point zero one mole adsorbed.

That distinction will matter when we change adsorbent mass. A lower uptake per kilogram does not automatically mean fewer total adsorbed moles. The total amount depends on both uptake and the amount of adsorbent present.

slides.title: Langmuir model
slides.narration:
The Langmuir equation writes uptake as the saturation uptake multiplied by b P, divided by one plus b P. Saturation uptake has units of moles per kilogram. The parameter b has reciprocal-pressure units, so the product b P is dimensionless.

The ratio of uptake to saturation uptake is the fractional coverage in this model. It rises from zero toward one as pressure increases. At b P equal to one, the coverage is one half.

The idealized interpretation involves a finite set of equivalent sites without lateral interactions. These assumptions help us understand the equation, but fitting the equation successfully does not establish a microscopic mechanism. Later, we will use it as a specified synthetic model and check its consequences through a vessel balance.

slides.title: Henry limit
slides.narration:
At sufficiently low pressure, b P is much smaller than one. The denominator of the Langmuir equation is then approximately one, so uptake becomes saturation uptake times b times pressure. This gives the Henry adsorption coefficient as saturation uptake multiplied by b.

With our chosen units, that coefficient is measured in moles per kilogram per kilopascal. A matched Henry line and Langmuir curve therefore share the same slope as pressure approaches zero. They do not necessarily agree at finite pressure.

The word Henry also appears in gas-solubility equations, sometimes written as partial pressure equals a constant times liquid mole fraction. That convention defines a different constant. Always state the equation, phases and concentration basis rather than relying on the name alone.

slides.title: Isotherm worked example
slides.narration:
Use the synthetic saturation uptake of two moles per kilogram and b equal to zero point one per kilopascal. Their product gives a Henry adsorption coefficient of zero point two moles per kilogram per kilopascal.

At one kilopascal, b P is zero point one. The Langmuir uptake is about zero point one eight one eight moles per kilogram, while the Henry value is zero point two. At ten kilopascals, b P equals one. Langmuir uptake is then one mole per kilogram, exactly half of its saturation uptake. The Henry line predicts two moles per kilogram.

This growing difference follows from the denominator in the Langmuir equation. Ten kilopascals is already well beyond a convincing small-b-P approximation for these parameters.

slides.title: Isotherm attempt
slides.narration:
Pause for about ten minutes and complete E one through E three on worksheet page four. Keep the same synthetic parameters and compare pressures of five and forty kilopascals.

Calculate both Langmuir and matched Henry uptake, then calculate Langmuir fractional coverage. Write the dimensionless product b P at each pressure. Use that product to judge the low-pressure assumption rather than deciding from the pressure number alone.

Finally, describe what each model predicts as pressure becomes large. Ask whether the equation contains a saturation limit and whether a mathematical value outside that limit is physically credible for the model's intended domain. Show the substitutions and units. Attempt the calculation before continuing to the comparison table on the next slide.

slides.title: Isotherm check
slides.narration:
At five kilopascals, b P is zero point five. Langmuir uptake is two thirds of a mole per kilogram, with coverage one third. The matched Henry line predicts one mole per kilogram.

At forty kilopascals, b P is four. Langmuir uptake is one point six moles per kilogram and coverage is zero point eight. The Henry value is eight moles per kilogram. That large value comes from extending a linear low-pressure expression into a range where its assumption is not satisfied.

Langmuir uptake approaches the specified saturation value of two moles per kilogram as pressure increases. The Henry equation has no plateau. The comparison illustrates model domains, rather than evidence that a real material actually follows either curve over this entire range.

slides.title: Closed adsorption vessel
slides.narration:
For a closed adsorption vessel, total adsorbate inventory equals gas moles plus adsorbed moles. The gas term is pressure times accessible gas volume divided by R T. The adsorbed term is adsorbent mass multiplied by absolute uptake.

Use the accessible gas volume in the ideal-gas term and convert adsorbent mass to kilograms before multiplying by uptake. The unknown pressure is the adsorbate partial pressure. At fixed temperature, volume, mass and inventory, the isotherm and this balance determine pressure together.

For positive Langmuir parameters, both amount terms increase with nonnegative pressure, giving a single nonnegative solution. The balance uses absolute uptake. An excess-adsorption measurement needs a density and volume convention before it can replace that quantity.

slides.title: Vessel worked example
slides.narration:
This worked example starts with a known pressure, rather than a known total inventory. At ten kilopascals, with saturation uptake two and b equal to zero point one per kilopascal, the Langmuir uptake is one mole per kilogram.

Ten grams is zero point zero one kilograms, so adsorbed moles equal zero point zero one. The gas amount in one liter at three hundred kelvin is about four point zero zero nine millimoles. Adding them gives a required total inventory of about zero point zero one four zero zero nine moles.

The next task reduces total inventory to zero point zero one mole while keeping the other parameters fixed. Do not carry the ten-kilopascal pressure across unchanged. It must satisfy the new balance.

The file is read by the browser and the saved cases become available to restore. Keep the actual file on your computer with the worksheet. An in memory comparison alone may disappear when you leave the page. Saving a screenshot is useful for discussion, but it cannot replace the inputs, units, model selection, and interpretation needed to reproduce the calculation. The plot range should also return to the saved zero to ten kilopascals. Restoring inputs is not the final calculation step. Press Compare and solve vessel to calculate the current state. If you edit any parameter after restoration, calculate again before treating the displayed result as evidence for that new case. The restored and recalculated Langmuir case again gives approximately six point zero eight zero kilopascals and the same gas and adsorbed amounts as before. This completes the full workflow from choosing a model to saving and reopening the result. In worksheet section G, reproduce the three cases yourself and verify each balance by hand. Explain why more adsorbent can increase the total adsorbed amount while decreasing uptake per kilogram. State the absolute uptake basis and the ideal gas assumption. The next activity stop gives you time to create and check your own evidence.

slides.title: Adsorption evidence
slides.narration:
A useful comparison needs more than a screenshot of a curve. Record the selected model, units and temperature because they define the meaning of each parameter. Then record pressure and uptake separately from the gas and adsorbed amounts.

The uptake is measured per kilogram, while the vessel balance uses moles. Check the mass conversion explicitly. The sum of gas moles and adsorbed moles should reproduce the chosen inventory, within rounding and numerical precision.

Keep a saved study and verify that reopening and recalculating it reproduces the result. Remember that two models can share a low-pressure slope without agreeing over the full range. Also, a correct numerical inventory balance verifies the calculation, but it does not prove that the chosen isotherm accurately represents a real material.

slides.title: Lab 11 independent investigation
slides.narration:
Pause for about twenty-four minutes and complete G one through G four on worksheet page five. Open Lab eleven and follow Lab guide pages three and four.

Run three cases with the same temperature, accessible volume and total inventory. Case eleven A uses Langmuir with ten grams of adsorbent. Case eleven B uses the matched Henry model with the same mass. Case eleven C returns to Langmuir and uses twenty grams.

Record pressure, uptake, gas moles and adsorbed moles, then check each balance with your calculator. Compare the findings with your predictions and inspect the graph. Save your studies, reopen one, verify its controls and calculate again. Explain the difference between uptake per kilogram and total adsorbed amount when interpreting the mass change.

slides.title: Lab 11 check
slides.narration:
The Langmuir case with ten grams gives about six point zero eight zero kilopascals. With the same inventory and mass, the matched Henry model gives about four point one six five kilopascals. Henry predicts more uptake at a common positive pressure, so it reaches this fixed inventory at a lower pressure.

Returning to Langmuir and increasing mass to twenty grams lowers pressure to about two point eight four five kilopascals. Uptake per kilogram decreases, but total adsorbed moles increase because there is more adsorbent.

Check the gas and adsorbed amounts in each row. Their sum is zero point zero one mole. The Henry result is useful for model sensitivity, but its finite b-P value requires caution about the low-pressure approximation.

slides.title: Model scope
slides.narration:
The Lab includes additional models and analysis options, but they need their own assumptions. Freundlich is an empirical expression over a stated pressure range and has no saturation plateau. BET uses relative pressure and requires a justified fitting range and reference pressure.

Isosteric heat requires comparing pressures at the same absolute loading across temperatures. Comparing arbitrary points on separate isotherms is not enough. Experimental fitting also needs measured data, uncertainty, units and a clear objective.

Today's examples use synthetic parameters to examine equilibrium and inventory reasoning. They do not establish an adsorption mechanism or validate extrapolation. You can explore the extensions later, but no new fit, BET calculation or isosteric-heat calculation is required to complete this lesson. Choose one relevant limitation for your reflection.

slides.title: Unseen case brief
slides.narration:
The final calculation transfers the method to new parameters. Keep the worked solutions closed and read H one through H four on worksheet page six.

For the gas-solid case, use three hundred and ten kelvin, two liters and a sublimation pressure of five kilopascals. Compare volatile inventories of zero point zero zero two and zero point zero zero eight moles. Add zero point zero zero one mole of inert gas to each.

For adsorption, use a different synthetic material with saturation uptake three moles per kilogram and b equal to zero point zero five per kilopascal. At twenty kilopascals and three hundred and ten kelvin, use two liters of accessible gas volume and five grams of adsorbent. Calculate the inventory required by that state.

slides.title: Unseen attempt
slides.narration:
Pause for about twenty minutes and complete H one through H four. Use the equations from the earlier slides, but make your own calculation before opening the answers.

For gas-solid equilibrium, determine the gas capacity first. Then find gas and solid amounts, volatile partial pressure and total pressure with the inert included. Check the species inventory in each case.

For adsorption, evaluate the isotherm at the specified pressure. Convert five grams to kilograms, then calculate gas moles, adsorbed moles and total inventory. Predict what happens to pressure if adsorbent mass doubles while that inventory stays fixed. An exact new pressure is not required. Finally, state one shared assumption and one difference between bulk gas-solid equilibrium and surface adsorption.

slides.title: Unseen check
slides.narration:
The gas capacity is approximately zero point zero zero three eight eight zero moles. The smaller volatile inventory therefore completely vaporizes. The larger inventory leaves about zero point zero zero four one two zero moles of solid and maintains a volatile partial pressure of five kilopascals.

The inert contribution is about one point two eight nine kilopascals. Add it to obtain the total pressures shown. For adsorption, uptake at twenty kilopascals is one point five moles per kilogram. Gas moles are about zero point zero one five five one nine, and adsorbed moles are zero point zero zero seven five. Their sum is about zero point zero two three zero one nine moles. Doubling adsorbent mass at that fixed inventory lowers pressure.

slides.title: Choosing an equilibrium description
slides.narration:
Use these four questions whenever you approach a new equilibrium problem. First, identify the physical process. Bulk phase transfer, surface uptake and chemical reaction require different descriptions.

Second, state the constraints. Temperature and pressure are not interchangeable with temperature and accessible volume. Third, identify the model and its conventions, including standard states, gas ideality, uptake basis, units and pressure range.

Finally, use material balances to determine amounts and check whether the proposed phases are actually present. A solubility composition, a sublimation pressure or an isotherm loading supplies only part of the description. None replaces an inventory balance. In your reflection, report a numerical result with its units, one supporting check and the assumptions needed for the interpretation. That combination makes the result useful and reproducible.
